grade.first_issue: After correctly writing the two circumcentre equations, the submission gives an undefined and generally incorrect formula for O and never derives the required dot-product identity; it merely attributes it to “symmetry.” This is an unsupported central inference under Rule E.
grade.summary: The solution makes meaningful analytic progress: it correctly reduces OM=ON to a linear identity involving O, B, and C, obtains useful sine-law relations for the directions of K and L, and states the correct linear circumcentre equations. However, it does not perform the essential compatibility/elimination showing that the angle conditions force the required identity. The closing assertion that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of MN is essentially the desired conclusion rather than a proof. Thus Rule E caps the score at 3.
strengths: Correctly derives that OM=ON is equivalent to O·(C-B)=(|C|^2-|B|^2)/4.
Correctly states 2O·k=|k|^2 and 2O·l=|l|^2 from the circumcentre condition.
The sine-law computations leading formally to cot(theta_K)=2cot(gamma)+cot(alpha) and cot(theta_L)=2cot(beta)+cot(alpha) provide relevant partial progress.

errors.description: No proof is supplied that the derived angle and length relations imply the required dot-product identity. The appeal to symmetry does not establish this highly nontrivial compatibility statement.
The displayed purported formula for O uses an undefined vector n-hat, has both terms in the same direction, and is not a valid general solution of the two circumcentre equations.
The final geometric description invokes an undefined point P and an unexplained coordinate component, so it cannot justify that O lies on the perpendicular bisector of MN.
The intermediate tangent formulas divide by tangents without treating admissible right-angle cases, although the corresponding cotangent identities can be derived without those divisions.
